A common mistake is logging structured data inconsistently: one service names the field user_id, another names it userId, making cross-service aggregation queries require normalisation. Agreeing on a shared logging schema across all services — ideally via a shared logging library — is a prerequisite for effective structured log queries.
words.connector: Think of structured logging like standardised forms rather than written letters — a custom letter describes a situation in free prose that only a human can interpret; a standardised form has named fields that a computer can process, aggregate, and search across thousands of submissions instantly.
words.techContext: After enforcing structured logging with consistent field names across all 25 services, our on-call time to diagnose incidents dropped from 25 minutes (grepping across unstructured logs) to under 5 minutes (Loki query by trace_id).
words.exampleSentence: Structured logging revealed that the payment timeouts were concentrated in requests from one specific client SDK version — a pattern that would have taken hours to find in unstructured log text.

codeExample.code:
# Structured logging with consistent fields
import structlog
from opentelemetry import trace

log = structlog.get_logger()

def process_order(order_id: str, user_id: str):
    span = trace.get_current_span()
    ctx = span.get_span_context()

    log.info(
        'order_processing_started',
        # Consistent fields across all services:
        service='order-service',
        environment='production',
        trace_id=format(ctx.trace_id, '032x'),
        order_id=order_id,
        user_id=user_id,
    )

words.etymology: Structured from Latin structura ('arrangement, building'); logging from the nautical ship's log (a sequential record); structured logging as a term emerged alongside JSON-based log aggregation platforms (Logstash/ELK stack) circa 2012.

words.shortDefinition: A translation boundary preventing one bounded context's model from polluting another's domain model.
words.simpleDefinition: An anti-corruption layer (ACL) is a translation layer placed between two subsystems with different domain models. It converts the external system's concepts and data shapes into the local model's language and structures, shielding the local domain from being forced to adopt the external model's vocabulary. Without an ACL, integrating a legacy system or external API causes its model to leak into your domain code.
words.longDefinition: The anti-corruption layer was introduced in Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design (2003) as the DDD solution to integration with systems using different domain models. In a microservices context, an ACL appears wherever a service must integrate with an external service (a legacy system, a third-party API, or a service from another bounded context) whose model vocabulary does not match the local model. The ACL translates incoming data from the external model to the local model, and translates outgoing requests from the local model to the external format. Without an ACL, a service that consumes an external 'Customer' object with 40 fields and its own naming conventions will gradually adopt those conventions in its own code — this is the corruption the pattern prevents. An ACL is typically implemented as a set of adapter objects and translation functions at the outermost layer of the service: repository adapters (translate database rows to domain objects), API client adapters (translate external API responses to local types), or anti-corruption services (a dedicated service that owns the translation). The ACL is particularly important at the boundaries of a strangler fig migration: the new service defines its own clean model, and the ACL handles translation with the legacy system until the legacy system is retired.
words.connector: Think of an anti-corruption layer like a professional translator at a diplomatic meeting — both parties speak in their own language and the translator ensures meaning is preserved without either party having to learn the other's vocabulary.
words.techContext: Our anti-corruption layer translates the legacy ERP's 'client_num' and 'acct_cd' fields into our domain's 'customerId' and 'accountType' before they reach any business logic, keeping the ERP's naming conventions outside our domain model.
words.exampleSentence: The anti-corruption layer protected the new inventory service from adopting the legacy WMS system's 30-year-old data model — instead of 'ITMNBR' and 'WHSCD', the domain used 'productId' and 'warehouseCode' throughout.

codeExample.code:
# Anti-Corruption Layer: translate legacy ERP response to domain model
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Order:              # Local domain model
    order_id: str
    customer_id: str
    total_amount: float

class LegacyErpAdapter:   # ACL — translation only, no business logic
    def __init__(self, legacy_client):
        self._client = legacy_client

    def get_order(self, order_id: str) -> Order:
        raw = self._client.fetch_ord(order_id)  # legacy API
        return Order(
            order_id=raw['ORD_NBR'],            # translate naming
            customer_id=raw['CUST_CD'],
            total_amount=float(raw['TOT_AMT']),
        )

words.etymology: Anti-corruption from the metaphor of preventing the 'corruption' (distortion) of one bounded context's model by another's vocabulary; coined and defined by Eric Evans in Domain-Driven Design (Addison-Wesley, 2003).

words.shortDefinition: Merging overly fine-grained services back into a cohesive module when the decomposition delivers no real benefit.
words.simpleDefinition: Service consolidation is the deliberate reversal of microservice decomposition: merging multiple services back into a larger, cohesive service or module when the decomposition is delivering no business or operational value. It is the anti-nanoservice correction. Consolidation candidates are services that always deploy together, always fail together, have no independent scaling requirements, and whose cross-service API is adding network latency and distributed transaction complexity with no architectural benefit.
words.longDefinition: Service consolidation is an underappreciated practice in the microservices lifecycle — the field's default story is decomposition and extraction, not consolidation. By 2024–2026, organisations that had over-decomposed published post-mortems describing consolidation back to modular monoliths or larger-grained service clusters as a net positive outcome. Consolidation indicators: two services that always deploy in the same release (they are not independently deployable in practice); services with shared transactional state (they are forced to use distributed transactions or accept inconsistency because they were decomposed at the wrong boundary); services where the latency of the cross-service call is the dominant performance characteristic (the network call costs more than the computation); services with no independent scaling profile (they always scale together). The consolidation process is the reverse of extraction: define the new cohesive module's boundary, inline the two services' logic into a single codebase, remove the network layer and replace it with in-process calls, migrate the data stores if they were separate. Consolidation does not mean abandoning module boundaries — the merged service can still have clear internal module structure enforced by tooling.
words.connector: Think of service consolidation like merging two neighbouring shops that always share a delivery truck, the same supplier, and the same customer base — the separation costs more in overhead than it provides in independence.
words.techContext: We consolidated our 'order-header' and 'order-line-items' services — they had always deployed together, shared a database schema, and the network call between them was causing 12ms of latency with no independent scaling benefit.
words.exampleSentence: Service consolidation of three user-profile services into one reduced deployment complexity by 70% and eliminated a class of cross-service race conditions that had taken weeks to debug.
words.etymology: Consolidation from Latin consolidare ('to make solid, to strengthen by combining'); in the context of microservices architecture, the term was popularised in post-mortems published by organisations like Segment (2020) and Amazon (Prime Video, 2023) that had over-decomposed.

words.shortDefinition: A security model where no service is trusted by default — every call is authenticated and authorised regardless of origin.
words.simpleDefinition: Zero-trust networking abandons the perimeter security model — where services inside the cluster trusted each other — in favour of continuous verification: every service-to-service call is authenticated (mTLS proves identity) and authorised (policy checks whether the caller is permitted to perform the requested operation) regardless of whether the caller is inside or outside the cluster. Compromise of one pod does not grant access to any other service.
words.longDefinition: The traditional perimeter security model assumed that traffic inside the data center or cluster was trustworthy — a hard outer shell protecting a soft interior. Microservices break this model: a cluster may contain hundreds of services from multiple teams, and a compromised pod inside the cluster has direct network access to all other pods. Zero-trust networking, formalised by John Kindervag at Forrester (2010) and operationalised for microservices via service meshes, applies the principle of least privilege to every service-to-service call. Concretely: every service has a cryptographic identity (SPIFFE SVID, provisioned by the mesh control plane); every inter-service connection uses mTLS (the sidecar or ztunnel negotiates certificate exchange transparently); every request is checked against an authorization policy (AuthorizationPolicy in Istio; Cilium NetworkPolicy) that explicitly permits the calling service to access the destination service on the requested path and method. Default-deny is the policy baseline: if no explicit allow rule exists, the call is rejected. Zero-trust principles extend beyond the service mesh to include secret access (every service authenticates to Vault with a short-lived token before retrieving secrets), cluster-to-cloud API calls (workload identity instead of long-lived API keys), and human access (engineers authenticate per-session rather than relying on VPN membership).
words.connector: Think of zero-trust networking like a secure government facility where every door requires a badge scan and a biometric — there is no interior corridor where you stop checking IDs because 'they already made it past the front desk'.
words.techContext: After enforcing zero-trust with Istio STRICT mTLS and AuthorizationPolicies, a compromised pod in our analytics namespace could no longer reach any service in the payments namespace — the lateral movement that would have enabled a credential theft was blocked at the network layer.
words.exampleSentence: Zero-trust networking stopped the post-breach analysis from being a multi-week forensic effort — every service call was authenticated and logged, so the blast radius of the compromised pod was reconstructed in under an hour.

codeExample.code:
# Istio AuthorizationPolicy: zero-trust default-deny + explicit allow
# Step 1: Deny all traffic in the payments namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: payments
spec: {}  # empty spec = deny everything

---
# Step 2: Explicitly allow orders service to call payment-service
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-orders-to-payments
  namespace: payments
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payment-service
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals:
              - cluster.local/ns/orders/sa/order-service
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: [POST]
            paths: ["/v1/charges"]

words.etymology: Zero-trust from John Kindervag's 2010 Forrester Research paper 'No More Chewy Centers: Introducing the Zero Trust Model of Information Security'; networking as the application domain; popularised in the cloud-native context by NIST SP 800-207 (2020) and service mesh implementations.
